title: Four Daily Routines
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: How people spend their time says a great deal about their lives. Researchers who study this subject often ask volunteers to keep a diary of everything they do in a normal day, and they then show the results as a circle divided into slices, each one representing a share of the twenty-four hours. This passage describes four people and their daily routines. Their circles look quite different, even though each person has exactly the same amount of time. All four agreed to be described by their first names, and all four kept their diaries for a full month, so that the figures do not depend on a single unusual day.

Dilnoza is a student in her final year at school. She divides her day into three equal parts: one third for sleep, one third for lessons and homework, and one third for everything else, including meals, travelling, friends and rest. She says that this pattern is not accidental, because she planned it carefully at the beginning of the year, and it has helped her to remain calm during the busy weeks before her examinations.

Bahodir is a doctor in a city hospital. Half of his day is spent at work, and the other half is divided equally between sleep and everything else. When he is on night duty, the pattern changes, but over a month the average is close to this. He admits that there is little time left for hobbies, and that he sometimes sleeps for only five hours. He would like to work fewer hours, but there are not enough doctors in the hospital.

Madina runs a small farm outside the city. In the summer, she works from before sunrise until late in the evening, and about three quarters of her day goes to the farm, leaving only one quarter for sleep, meals and family. In winter, there is far less to do, and her circle looks completely different. She says that farming is not a job but a way of life, and that she accepts the long hours because she loves the work. Her children help at weekends and during the harvest, and she hopes that one of them will take over the farm when she is older.

Jasur is a retired teacher. His day has one large slice and four small, equal ones. The large slice, about sixty per cent of the day, is for sleep and rest, which he needs more than he used to, since he now gets tired more easily than he did when he was young and often takes a short nap after lunch. The small slices are for walking, reading, visiting neighbours and helping his grandchildren with their homework. He says that after a lifetime of rushing, he enjoys having time to do nothing in particular.

What do these circles show? According to Dr Karina Petrova, a researcher in time use, they show that the amount of time is the same for everybody, but that the choices are very different, and that these choices are shaped by age, work and the needs of family. She adds that people who are satisfied with their lives are not always those with the most free time, but those whose time is spent on activities that matter to them.

It can be useful to draw one's own circle. Many people are surprised to find how much time goes to activities that they did not choose, such as waiting, scrolling on a phone or travelling. Dr Petrova suggests keeping a diary for just one week and asking, at the end, which slices should be larger and which smaller. The exercise costs nothing, she says, and it often leads to small changes that make a surprising difference to a person's well-being.
